Issued at 400 AM CST Thu Nov 12 2026

A much cooler air mass will continue to spill into the Great 
Lakes region today as longwave troughing over eastern Canada 
becomes re-centered over the eastern Great Lakes and multiple 
embedded shortwave troughs along its western periphery nosedive 
southward from western Ontario towards northern Illinois. The 
00Z RAOBs from both GRB and APX last evening sampled an 850 mb 
temperature of around -1C, which isn't all that remarkable for 
this time of year at these RAOB sites. However, when paired with
lake temperatures that are still in the low-mid 50s (11-13C) 
and an elongated northerly fetch over Lake Michigan, this 
initial push of colder air has been cool enough for some 
relatively disorganized lake effect showers to stream into 
portions of northwest Indiana this morning.

The lake effect shower activity should steadily increase in 
coverage, organization, and overall intensity over the course of
the day today as 850 mb temperatures gradually fall towards and
eventually into the -5 to -7C range over Lake Michigan. By late
tonight, water surface-850 mb temperature differentials will be
nearing 20C, while water surface-700 mb temperature 
differentials will be pushing 30C. This will yield a deep 
convective cloud layer, with an analysis of HRRR and RAP 
forecast soundings in BUFKIT indicating that lake-induced CAPE 
values should largely remain at or above 500 J/kg through a 
large portion of this lake effect event, likely peaking 
somewhere around 700 J/kg towards midday Friday. With the 
northerly fetch over Lake Michigan not expected change much 
anytime soon, a prolonged lake effect precipitation event can be
expected for a portion of our forecast area from today through 
early Saturday, with the lake-induced thermodynamics supportive
of efficient precipitation rates at times and also a potential 
for waterspouts over Lake Michigan.

During the daytime today, air temperatures largely in the 40s 
will result in rain being the sole precipitation type. The 
latest hi-res model guidance suggests that the primary lake 
convergence axis will remain relatively steady with its position
and orientation through the daytime hours, which should focus 
most of today's lake effect showers into our northwest Indiana 
counties. This is in contrast to earlier model runs, which 
suggested that a large footprint of lake effect showers could 
penetrate well westward into Illinois, though areas roughly east
of I-355 in the Chicago metro and near/east of I-57 farther 
downstate may still nevertheless get in on the lake effect 
action at some point later this morning or afternoon. Still 
couldn't rule out a brief period of non-lake-induced convective 
showers or sprinkles farther to the west in interior portions of
northern Illinois, though moisture depth/quality will be a 
factor in limiting the spatial footprint of this activity. In 
addition, it should also be noted that blustery northerly winds 
are also expected throughout the day today, which will prevent 
temperatures from rising much above this morning's lows.

By this evening, a more dominant, singular lake effect 
precipitation band should emerge. Air temperatures will also 
fall into the low-mid 30s (and possibly into the mid-upper 20s 
wherever skies end up clearing out) after sunset as cold air 
advection continues, which will allow for the rain in the lake 
effect band to mix with and eventually change over to snow in 
most locations. The main exception to this may be in the 
immediate vicinity of the lakeshore, where the mild lake- 
influenced air advecting inland could potentially prevent an 
outright changeover to snow. Even in the most bullish/coldest 
hi-res models, though, near-surface wet bulb globe temperatures
aren't progged to fall much below 32F, which -- when paired 
with relatively mild antecedent ground temperatures -- would 
make it difficult for snow to accumulate, particularly on 
warmer paved surfaces.

In these scenarios, snowfall rates need to be fairly high in 
order to overcome the less-than-ideal thermal environment and 
lead to meaningful snow accumulation, and in this particular 
case, the lake effect band should be robust enough for at least 
lower-end localized slushy, wet snow accumulations to occur. In 
the worst case (which has been depicted in a handful of hi-res 
model runs, but not ubiquitously across the hi-res guidance 
suite), a localized "bullseye" of several inches of wet snow 
accumulation could occur somewhere if the band were to park 
itself and remain stationary over the same area. Confidence in 
such an outcome occurring in our CWA is low at this time, but 
it's certainly within the realm of possibilities at this point.

Not unsurprising for a lake effect setup like this, uncertainty
also remains with where the "average" position of the lake 
effect band will end up and how far west it will ultimately
wobble. It should be noted that hi-res models have been showing
